source.title: Vision-Language Asymmetry in Bistable Image Captioning

record.tranche_reason: Tests SAE-recoverable visual features and their caption effects in a vision-language model on bistable images, a new setting for the claim; it does not reproduce the original toy-network method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a behavioral baseline of 3,320 captions and prompt-dependent commitment, but that baseline does not itself measure feature recovery or superposition, so it is not included as a row. It also discusses results from other papers; those are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The paper uses 'superposition' in a different sense: both aspect-specific SAE feature pools co-activating on an ambiguous (bistable) image. It does not mean features stored in overlapping directions because of limited capacity. The TopK SAE is a tool for locating aspect-selective features, and those features are chosen by AUROC thresholds. Steering results measure caption flips, not feature storage. No result bears on whether models superpose sparse features, on polysemanticity, on whether SAE features are canonical, or on feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that both aspect feature pools usually co-activate in the CLIP vision tower, and that aspect commitment ('seeing-as') is made downstream in the language decoder. Steering flips default-dominant captions (33% rabbit) but not force-balanced young/old captions. They caveat that the result holds for one VLM and one SAE run without random-feature baselines. They also add a methodological note: rank statistics on TopK SAE outputs need tie-corrected ranking.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a TopK SAE on CLIP layer-22 patch activations, aspect-specific feature identification, and causal activation steering in a VLM. It is not the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies across image groups and steering direction/strength; duck-rabbit steering toward rabbit and hidden-face steering toward A shift some captions, whereas young-old steering yields no aspect-committed captions across the tested coefficients. The authors also state that prompt changes alter caption-level commitment.

fits_no_version.finding: On 50/69 bistable images, pools of SAE features selective for each aspect both fire above their opposite-control thresholds at CLIP layer 22 of LLaVA-1.6-7B. Steering with these pools flips captions on duck/rabbit (33%) but never on young/old (0/7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Competing interpretations of ambiguous images co-activate in a VLM's vision encoder, and caption commitment is made downstream in the language decoder.

record.code_released: Reproducibility: code, configs, and per-stimulus result tables will be released upon acceptance; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Evidence is limited to one VLM and a single SAE training run. The paper explicitly leaves cross-model and cross-SAE generalization and random-feature and permuted-aspect baselines to future work. The Schroeder stairs group has thin pure-B controls (n = 8). No error bars, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or p-values are reported for the cataloged results.
record.rows_left_out: None. All reported per-group feature-pool classifications and all per-direction, per-coefficient steering results in Appendix C, Table 2 are included.

untested.parts: No toy networks, no sparsity sweep, no transition or geometry.
No neuron-level capacity or polysemanticity analysis.
No analysis of the causes of polysemanticity.

The SAE is trained and used as a tool (validation EV 0.93). There is no test of whether features are distributed across neurons or of how sparse features are recovered, beyond selecting aspect-selective features.
No test of completeness, stability across runs, or canonicality; a single SAE run was used.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The overlap with the claim is terminological only: the paper's 'superposition' means co-activation of two interpretations, not capacity-driven overlap of feature directions. The reader's V4 links and labels should be dropped. The tie-corrected AUROC note (Appendix D: phantom features from stable-sort ties) is a methodological pitfall for SAE analyses, not a test of any version.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, dimensional-capacity sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric arrangement of feature directions.
Does not test competition for neuron capacity, dedicated dimensions for important features, or polysemanticity caused by capacity limits.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Tests sparse SAE-recovered visual features in one VLM's CLIP vision tower, not feature distribution across neurons or SAE features in language-model layers, other LLMs, or other training runs.
Does not establish that SAE features are complete, stable across runs, or canonical units; the authors explicitly leave cross-SAE generalization for future work.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-7B
rows.operation_detail: Identified per-aspect features with a TopK SAE trained on CLIP layer-22 patch activations; results summarized across six bistable-image groups.
rows.measure: Number of retained features per aspect; median leave-one-out AUROC and CC3M-distractor AUROC
rows.value: Exactly 15 features per aspect per group (30 per group; 180 overall); median leave-one-out AUROC ≥ 0.997 across all six groups and median CC3M-distractor AUROC ≥ 0.998.
rows.note: Features were selected using leave-one-out AUROC, a mean-match activation floor, and a distractor-specificity test. The result is for this SAE and this model's CLIP layer.
rows.check: These are selection values. Exactly 15 features per aspect is a cap the authors imposed, and the AUROCs are the filtering criteria. They describe the study's own feature-finding method, not evidence that the model stores sparse features in superposition.

rows.subject: LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-7B
rows.operation_detail: Measured simultaneous activation of the two per-aspect SAE feature pools on bistable stimuli.
rows.measure: Stimuli classified as superposition (both feature pools above their opposite-aspect-control thresholds)
rows.baseline: Opposite-aspect control median activation threshold for each pool
rows.note: All 12 stimuli were classified as superposition.
rows.check: The paper's 'superposition' label (both aspect pools above opposite-control median) is co-activation of two interpretations. That is a different construct from feature superposition in V1/V4, so 12/12 is not evidence on any version. The same applies to r3–r8.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-7B CLIP layer 22; six bistable-image groups
reader_labels.reason: The SAE retained per-aspect features with high reported discrimination, and both pools were above control thresholds for 50/69 stimuli overall; see r1–r8.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Single VLM, single SAE training run, and CLIP vision tower; steering outcomes across duck rabbit, hidden face, and young old woman
reader_labels.reason: The authors limit generalization to one VLM and one SAE run; steering was partial for some settings and absent for force-balanced young/old captions at every tested coefficient. The study does not establish feature distribution across LLM neurons or generality across models; see r9–r44.
